explanation: UMN lesion is characterized by spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski (dorsiflexion of big toe), and primitive reflexes; plantar flexion indicates a normal (intact) reflex.
LMN lesion is characterized by flaccid paralysis, muscle wasting, fasciculations, and decreased/absent reflexes; hypertonia, increased reflexes, and Babinski are UMN features, not LMN.
Syringomyelia expands in the central canal first, affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, causing bilateral suspended sensory loss for pain and temperature.
The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; crus cerebri is a midbrain structure containing corticospinal fibers.
The brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata, but NOT the cerebellum (which overlies the fourth ventricle as a separate structure) nor the cerebral aqueduct.
The cranial part of accessory nerve arises from nucleus ambiguus in the medulla, and its fibers join the vagus nerve to supply pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.
The right spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature from the LEFT side of the body, as the spinothalamic tract crosses at the spinal cord level before ascending.
Dorsal columns (gracile and cuneate) are supplied by posterior spinal arteries and radicular arteries; the vertebral artery supplies the brain stem but not spinal cord directly.
Lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace, below or above the tip of L4 spinous process, safely below where the spinal cord ends.
Complete transection above C5 causes quadriplegia due to interruption of all descending corticospinal, corticoreticulospinal, and rubrospinal tracts before they supply the limbs.
In hemisection, ipsilateral findings include proprioception loss (dorsal column) and UMN signs below the lesion; pain/temperature loss is contralateral (spinothalamic crossing).
Brown-Sequard syndrome has ipsilateral LMN signs at the level of lesion, NOT contralateral; LMN signs at the level occur on the same side as the lesion.
UMN lesion features: spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski, and loss of abdominal reflexes; options A, B, C describe LMN features (hypotonia, wasting, restricted paralysis).
LMN lesion causes flaccid paralysis with marked muscle wasting and absent reflexes; options A, B, C, E are UMN features (hypertonia, absent reflexes, hyperreflexia, Babinski).
Syringomyelia affects pain and temperature on BOTH sides first because the syrinx damages crossing fibers in the anterior white commissure before affecting other tracts.
Hindbrain includes medulla, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; crus cerebri is a midbrain structure (part of cerebral peduncle) that belongs to the mesencephalon.
Brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla; cerebellum is attached via peduncles but is not part of brain stem; cerebral aqueduct is CSF space within midbrain.
Cranial accessory nerve fibers originate from nucleus ambiguus and merge with vagus nerve; this is why the cranial component is sometimes considered part of CN X.
The right spinal lemniscus carries left-sided pain and temperature because spinothalamic fibers cross at their segmental level before ascending in the lemniscus.
Dorsal column tracts receive dual blood supply from posterior spinal arteries and radicular (dorsal root) arteries, providing collateral circulation.
The L4 spinous process is the key landmark for lumbar puncture; the L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace is used, as the conus medullaris ends at L1-L2 in adults.
Above C5 transection paralyzes all four limbs (quadriplegia) and may compromise respiration if the phrenic nerve nuclei (C3-C5) are affected; paraplegia would require a thoracic lesion.
Hemiation produces ipsilateral dorsal column loss (proprioception) and corticospinal signs (UMN), with contralateral spinothalamic loss; options A and B are both ipsilateral.
In Brown-Sequard, the LMN lesion at the same level is ipsilateral, not contralateral, due to anterior horn cell damage at the level of the lesion on the same side.
UMN signs include hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and Babinski (dorsiflexion); options A, B, C and normal plantar flexion are NOT UMN characteristics.
LMN signs include flaccidity, hyporeflexia, marked wasting, and fasciculations; hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and Babinski are UMN features not seen in LMN lesions.

Syringomyelia typically affects pain and temperature sensation first because the central canal expansion damages crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior commissure before affecting motor neurons.
